newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stock rally seen overshadowing Democratic meet.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stock rally seen overshadowing Democratic meet.

text.p: Tobacco shares are set to rally this week after a jury ruled in favour of four cigarette makers in a liability suit, overshadowing, so far as markets are concerned, the Democratic Convention kicking off Monday.

The Chicago gathering is considered by most Wall Street pros to be no more an event than its Republican counterpart in San Diego earlier this month unless the Democrats take up Republican Presidential nominee Bob Dole's gauntlet and begin promising sweeping tax cuts of their own.

In addition to tobacco shares, investors will eye auto stocks after the United Auto Workers delayed chosing a strike target among Detroit's Big Three and said it may try to hammer out new labour contracts with the companies simultaneously.
The week, expected to be sleepy as it winds its way toward the extended U.S. Labour Day weekend, will also see its share of economic data.
But the tobacco industry will the focus of interest, albeit on slim summer volume, after the Indianapolis court ruling which was announced late Friday evening.

"I would assume that Philip Morris will make it up into the mid-90," said Bill Lefevre, senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum. The stock closed at 88 on Friday before the verdict was known.
Analysts had said that the stock could have gone down to about 80 had the court ruled against the tobacco companies.

Lefevre said that in addition to the verdict, Philip Morris, which fell 17 points since an unfavourable ruling in a Florida court on Aug. 9, will get a push up this week because it is expected to announce another big dividend increase.
The Indianapolis suit was brought against the tobacco industry by the family of a man who died of lung cancer after smoking for more than 40 years.

The case, similar to hundreds that have been filed across the country, follows one earlier this month in Jacksonville, Fla., where a jury awarded $750,000 to a man who smoked for 44 years before he was stricken with lung cancer.
It had been a tough time for tobacco. Last Friday, President Clinton announced new rules to curb teenage smoking by restricting sales and marketing of tobacco.
Clinton will get his chance to reinforce or further narrow his lead over Dole when Democrats converge in Chicago for their national convention.

"The wild card here is if the Democrats get aggressive over tax cutting. If they get too generous and there is a bidding war to cut taxes without offsetting spending cuts, the bond market will get very nervous," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

Another point of interest this week is the auto industry. In an unprecedented move last week, the United Auto Workers put off chosing a strike target among Chrysler Corp., General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor. Co.
The UAW said that there may not be a need to target a company this year in what labour analysts said was a move to gain leverage in the union's favour.
"Wage settlements create the impression that the unions are getting stronger," said David Bostian, chief economist at Heine Herzog Geduld.
Metz added that the main problem for the auto industry remained higher interest rates which will increase the cost of buying autos.

Data this week include July existing homes on Monday, August consumer confidence on Tuesday, the second quarter real gross domestic product on Thursday, July new home sales on Thursday and Friday's personal income and consumption for July.
